questions.q: Compare the Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari and Mahalwari systems of land revenue.
answer: To secure a steady income, the Company introduced three main land-revenue systems.

answer.text: Introduced by Cornwallis in Bengal and Bihar, it made zamindars the owners of land and fixed their revenue permanently. Zamindars often failed to invest and oppressed the peasants.
Developed by Munro and Read for Madras and Bombay, it settled revenue directly with each ryot, or cultivator, without a zamindar in between.
Devised by Holt Mackenzie in 1822 for the North-Western Provinces, it settled revenue with the whole village, or mahal, as a unit, and the demand was revised from time to time.

answer: All three aimed to maximise revenue, and all pressed heavily on the peasantry.

questions.q: Describe the causes and outcome of the Indigo (Blue) Rebellion of 1859.

answer.text: European planters forced Bengal peasants to grow indigo, a blue dye in great demand in Europe, mainly under the ryoti system, in which ryots grew indigo on their own land under oppressive contracts and loans that trapped them in debt, while earning almost nothing.

In 1859 the indigo ryots of Bengal refused to grow the crop, attacked indigo factories and boycotted those who worked for planters. They were supported by many zamindars, the local press and some officials.

The government appointed the Indigo Commission in 1860, which held the planters guilty, and indigo cultivation collapsed in Bengal. It shifted to Bihar, where Gandhi later led the Champaran movement in 1917.

questions.q: Why did the Company want to grow indigo, and how was it cultivated under the ryoti and nij systems?

answer.text: Indigo produced a rich blue dye prized by European cloth manufacturers. As demand soared and other sources dried up, India — especially Bengal and Bihar — became the main supplier, and planters pushed to expand cultivation.
meant the planter grew indigo on land he directly controlled — bought or rented — using hired labourers. It needed large areas, ploughs and bullocks, so it stayed limited.

Prices paid were low and debts never cleared, trapping peasants in a cycle of loans
Indigo also exhausted the soil, harming the next crop

questions.q: What was the Permanent Settlement, and what problems did it create for the Company and the peasants?

answer.text: the Permanent Settlement made rajas and taluqdars into zamindars who collected rent from peasants and paid a fixed revenue to the Company. The amount was fixed permanently, so it would never rise.

list: The Company hoped a fixed demand would give it steady income and create loyal, investing landlords
But the demand was set so high that zamindars who failed to pay lost their lands
As prices and cultivation rose, the Company lost out because its share stayed fixed
Zamindars had little incentive to improve land; peasants faced high rents and harsh terms
